questoes.pergunta: Which statement best describes the difference between prompt-based guidance and a programmatic prerequisite for enforcing tool order in an agent?
opcoes: A prerequisite is a logging hook that records out-of-order calls for review; prompt guidance is what actually prevents them.
With few-shot examples of the right order, prompt guidance reaches the same reliability as a prerequisite at lower cost.
Prompt guidance makes the right order likely but keeps a non-zero failure rate; a prerequisite blocks the wrong order every time.
A programmatic prerequisite is a stronger form of prompt guidance that places the required order inside each of the tools' descriptions.
questoes.explicacao: Instructions in the prompt produce probabilistic compliance: they raise the odds of the right order but never reach zero failures. A programmatic prerequisite (a hook or gate) runs on every call and blocks the out-of-order step deterministically, which is what a mandatory sequence such as identity verification before a refund requires.
feedbacks: Tempting because many hooks do log, but a prerequisite blocks the out-of-order call; monitoring only records the violation after it happens, and the prompt is the probabilistic part.
Few-shot examples improve consistency, but they remain prompt-based guidance with a non-zero failure rate; only the prerequisite blocks the wrong order every time.
Correct. Prompt guidance is probabilistic; a programmatic prerequisite is deterministic.
A tool description is still text the model reads, so it is guidance, not enforcement. A prerequisite is code that blocks the call.

questoes.pergunta: In the customer support agent, a programmatic prerequisite guards process_refund. What should unlock the refund call?
opcoes: A get_customer result earlier in this session that returned a verified customer ID matching the refund's customer.
The model stating in its reasoning that it already verified the customer's identity in an earlier turn.
A lookup_order call that returned the order, since an order lookup implies that the customer was identified.
The customer's name and email typed in the conversation, matched by the model against the order's billing data.
questoes.explicacao: The prerequisite should depend on the result of the prerequisite tool, not on what the model says. Blocking process_refund until get_customer has returned a verified customer ID, and checking that the refund targets that ID, is the pattern the exam guide describes.
feedbacks: Correct. The gate unlocks on get_customer's verified result for the same customer.
A self-declaration is exactly what the gate exists to avoid; the model can state it verified when it did not.
An order lookup does not verify identity; the official example blocks lookup_order too until get_customer has run.
Matching typed details is the model's own heuristic, not a verified result from the identity tool.

questoes.pergunta: A customer writes: "My headphones arrived broken, I was charged twice for my subscription, and my coupon didn't apply." What is the recommended way for the agent to handle this message?
opcoes: Resolve the broken headphones first, then ask the customer to open a separate new conversation for each of the other two issues.
Escalate the whole conversation to a human, because a message with several separate issues is too complex for the agent.
Handle the issues one at a time in the order written, confirming each resolution with the customer before the next one starts.
Split it into three items, investigate them in parallel using the shared customer context, then send one unified resolution.
questoes.explicacao: Multi-concern requests should be decomposed into distinct items, each investigated in parallel using shared context (the verified customer and their orders), and then synthesized into one resolution. That is faster than a sequential flow and keeps the answers consistent.
feedbacks: It pushes work back onto the customer and loses the shared context between the issues.
Several issues do not make a case an escalation; complexity alone is not a trigger, and each item here is within the agent's scope.
Sequential handling works but is slow and makes the customer confirm repeatedly; the issues are independent and can be investigated in parallel.
Correct. Decompose, investigate in parallel with shared context, then give one unified resolution.

questoes.pergunta: An agent escalates a refund case to a human who cannot see the conversation. Which handoff content does the exam guide call for?
opcoes: The full conversation transcript, so the human has each message and can decide what matters for the case.
The customer ID, root cause, refund amount, and recommended action, each as a structured field.
A short free-text paragraph that describes the problem, written in the agent's own words for readability.
A structured record of the customer's sentiment and the agent's confidence, so the human can prioritize it.
questoes.explicacao: When the human lacks the transcript, the handoff must be a structured summary with what is needed to act: customer ID, root cause, refund amount, and recommended action. That avoids re-investigation and re-contacting the customer.
feedbacks: A transcript hands the human a document to read instead of a case to act on, and the key facts still have to be dug out.
Correct. These are the fields the guide lists for a structured handoff.
Free text is better than nothing but tends to omit the ID, the amount, or the recommended action.
Sentiment and self-reported confidence do not tell the human what happened or what to do.

questoes.pergunta: What does a PostToolUse hook in the Claude Agent SDK let you do?
opcoes: Transform a tool's result after the tool runs and before the model processes it, for example to normalize formats.
Block a tool call before it runs when its arguments break a policy, for example a refund above a set limit for the agent.
Re-run a tool with corrected arguments whenever the first call returns an error, before the agent sees the result.
Change which tool the model will select next, based on the result of the tool that has just finished running.
questoes.explicacao: PostToolUse hooks intercept tool results after execution and can transform them before the model processes them, for example to normalize timestamps or mask sensitive data. Blocking a call before it runs is the job of tool call interception (PreToolUse).
feedbacks: Correct. PostToolUse transforms results before the model sees them.
That is interception of the outgoing call, which happens in PreToolUse; by the time PostToolUse runs, the tool has executed.
Hooks transform or block; deciding to retry with new arguments is part of the agent's loop, not a PostToolUse feature.
Tool selection stays with the model; a hook can change what the model reads, not pick its next tool.

questoes.pergunta: Three MCP tools return dates as Unix timestamps, ISO 8601 strings with offsets, and numeric status codes. One of the servers is third-party. Where is normalization most reliable?
opcoes: In the system prompt, with conversion rules written out for each tool's format.
In a PreToolUse hook that converts each tool's date arguments before it runs.
In a PostToolUse hook that converts every tool result before the model processes it.
In each MCP server, by asking each vendor to switch their output to ISO 8601.
questoes.explicacao: A PostToolUse hook normalizes heterogeneous formats deterministically, on every call, before the agent processes the data. It works even for servers you cannot modify, and it does not depend on the model remembering a rule.
feedbacks: Conversion rules in the prompt depend on the model applying them correctly every time, which is probabilistic.
Right mechanism, wrong side: PreToolUse changes the arguments going out, but the mixed formats are in the results coming back.
Correct. PostToolUse normalization is deterministic and works for third-party servers.
You do not control a third-party server, and waiting on vendors is not a reliable or quick fix.

questoes.pergunta: Policy says refunds above $500 need human approval. Which hook design enforces this and keeps the workflow moving?
opcoes: A PostToolUse hook on process_refund that alerts a supervisor whenever an issued refund is above the $500 limit.
A PreToolUse hook on process_refund that denies calls above $500 and tells the agent to call escalate_to_human.
A PreToolUse hook that denies every process_refund call and sends each refund request to escalate_to_human.
A PostToolUse hook on lookup_order that adds a note telling the model not to refund more than $500 for that order.
questoes.explicacao: Tool call interception (PreToolUse) can block a policy-violating action before it happens and redirect the agent to an alternative workflow such as human escalation. Refunds within the limit still go through automatically.
feedbacks: PostToolUse runs after the refund has been issued; it can report the violation but not prevent it.
Correct. Intercept the call, deny above the threshold, and redirect to escalation.
It enforces the limit by removing all automation, which sends easy refunds to humans and hurts first-contact resolution.
A note in the result is still guidance the model may not follow; it does not block the refund call.

questoes.pergunta: Which of these business rules most clearly calls for a hook instead of a prompt instruction?
opcoes: Greet returning customers by name and keep each reply under 120 words.
Offer the extended warranty when the customer seems interested in it.
Use a friendly tone and avoid technical jargon with first-time buyers.
Never send a refund to an account other than the verified one.
questoes.explicacao: Hooks give deterministic guarantees, so they fit rules that require guaranteed compliance, such as financial or identity rules. Tone, length, and judgment calls are best handled with prompt instructions, where occasional deviation is acceptable.
feedbacks: A style rule: occasional deviations are acceptable, so a prompt instruction is the proportionate tool.
This needs judgment about the customer's interest, which a prompt handles well and a hook cannot evaluate.
Tone is best-effort guidance; enforcing it with a hook would be over-engineering.
Correct. A financial rule that must always hold calls for deterministic enforcement in code.

questoes.pergunta: Which TWO situations are appropriate escalation triggers for the customer support agent? Choose TWO.
opcoes: The conversation has passed 20 turns while the agent works through a long multi-item return request.
The customer asks for a price match with a competitor, and the policy covers only own-site price changes.
The agent rates its own confidence in the resolution it is about to propose at 5 out of 10.
The customer says they want to talk to a person instead of continuing with the agent.
The customer writes in capital letters and uses strong language about a delivery that is two days late.
questoes.explicacao: Appropriate triggers are an explicit request for a human, a policy exception or gap, and an inability to make progress. Strong language, conversation length, and self-reported confidence are poor proxies for whether the case actually needs a human.
feedbacks: Length alone is not a trigger; long cases that are fully covered by the policy should still be resolved.
Correct. The policy is silent on competitor price matching, which is a policy gap.
Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated and is not a reliable escalation trigger.
Correct. An explicit request for a human is honored immediately.
Sentiment is not complexity: an angry customer with a late delivery is a case the agent can resolve.

questoes.pergunta: Mid-conversation, a customer writes: "I'd like to speak with a human, please." The agent is fairly sure it could solve the issue in one more turn. What should it do?
opcoes: Solve the issue in one more turn, then offer the transfer if the customer still wants it.
Explain that it can resolve this faster and ask the customer to confirm the transfer request.
Escalate right away with a structured handoff, without investigating the issue any further.
Look up the order first, so the structured handoff includes a full diagnosis of the issue.
questoes.explicacao: An explicit request for a human is honored immediately, without first attempting investigation or a resolution. The agent passes along what it already knows in a structured handoff.
feedbacks: It overrides the customer's explicit preference to chase first-contact resolution.
Asking for confirmation pushes back on a request the customer already made clearly.
Correct. Honor the explicit request immediately, with a handoff.
Investigating first delays the transfer the customer asked for; send what is already known.

questoes.pergunta: A frustrated customer complains about a damaged item that the policy covers with a replacement. They do not ask for a human. What should the agent do?
opcoes: Acknowledge the frustration and offer the replacement, escalating only if the customer then asks again for a human.
Escalate at once, because strong frustration shows the case needs a human's judgment and empathy to resolve.
Set the tone aside and process the replacement without comment, since tone does not change the policy.
Add an automatic goodwill discount to the replacement, since frustration signals a risk of churn.
questoes.explicacao: When the issue is within the agent's capability, it should acknowledge the frustration and offer the resolution, escalating only if the customer reiterates a preference for a human.
feedbacks: Correct. Acknowledge, offer the in-policy resolution, and escalate if the customer reiterates.
Frustration is not complexity; escalating a straightforward, in-policy case lowers first-contact resolution.
Resolving is right, but skipping the acknowledgment ignores the customer and leaves no path if they ask for a person.
A discount the policy does not define is the agent improvising compensation; acknowledge the frustration, offer the in-policy fix, and escalate if the customer reiterates.

questoes.pergunta: A retailer's policy covers price adjustments when the price drops on its own website. A customer asks the agent to match a competitor's lower price. What should the agent do?
opcoes: Apply the website adjustment rule by analogy, since the customer would get the same outcome.
Escalate, because the policy is silent on matching a competitor's price for this item.
Decline, because the policy does not list competitor prices among the cases that it covers.
Offer a small goodwill credit as a compromise, then close the case as resolved.
questoes.explicacao: When the policy is ambiguous or silent on the customer's specific request, the agent should escalate. Competitor price matching when the policy addresses only own-site adjustments is the exam guide's own example.
feedbacks: Extending a rule by analogy means the agent is creating policy it has no authority to set.
Correct. A policy gap is an escalation trigger.
Reading silence as a refusal is also a policy decision the agent is not authorized to make.
A compromise is still an improvised exception the policy does not define.

questoes.pergunta: Why is customer sentiment a poor trigger for escalating a support conversation?
opcoes: It fires too late, since frustration shows up only after the customer has already given up.
It is too noisy on short messages, so it first needs to be averaged over several turns.
It ignores the agent's own confidence score, which is a better signal of how hard the case is.
It measures emotion, not whether the case actually needs a human's authority.
questoes.explicacao: Sentiment-based escalation is an unreliable proxy for case complexity: an angry customer may have a trivial, in-policy issue, while a calm customer may need a policy exception.
feedbacks: Timing is not the issue: even an instant, perfectly timed sentiment signal still measures mood, so a calm customer who needs a policy exception is never escalated.
Averaging makes the signal steadier, not more relevant: an angry customer with a trivial in-policy issue still gets escalated.
Self-reported confidence is also an unreliable proxy for case complexity, so swapping one proxy for another does not fix the trigger.
Correct. Emotion and case complexity are different things: the triggers that matter are an explicit request, a policy gap, or no progress.

questoes.pergunta: get_customer returns two accounts named Ana Lima, both with recent orders. What should the agent do?
opcoes: Pick the account with the most recent order, which is the most likely match.
List both accounts with their emails so the customer can choose the right one.
Ask for an additional identifier, such as the order number or the account email.
Escalate to a human, since ambiguity about who the customer is needs a person.
questoes.explicacao: Multiple customer matches require clarification with an additional identifier rather than heuristic selection. The agent can resolve the ambiguity itself, without guessing and without exposing other customers' data.
feedbacks: Recency is a heuristic; a wrong pick acts on someone else's account.
It involves the customer but exposes another customer's email; asking for an identifier avoids the leak.
Correct. Ask for an additional identifier before acting.
The agent can resolve this with one question, so escalation lowers first-contact resolution needlessly.

questoes.pergunta: A support agent escalates many simple in-policy cases and handles some policy-exception requests on its own. What is the most proportionate first fix?
opcoes: Add explicit escalation criteria to the system prompt, with few-shot examples of escalate versus resolve.
Train a classifier on past tickets to decide which conversations should be sent to a human agent.
Add an explicit rule to escalate whenever the agent's self-reported confidence drops below 7 of 10.
Add a hook that escalates every conversation in which a refund or a policy exception is mentioned by the customer.
questoes.explicacao: Poor escalation calibration comes from unclear decision boundaries. Explicit criteria with few-shot examples in the system prompt address that directly and are the proportionate first step before adding infrastructure.
feedbacks: Correct. Explicit escalation criteria with few-shot examples are the first fix for miscalibrated escalation.
Over-engineering: it needs labeled data and ML infrastructure before the prompt has been improved.
Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated; the agent is often confident on exactly the hard cases.
Escalation here is a judgment call; a keyword hook would escalate many resolvable refunds and still miss unstated exceptions.
